Dry eyes

A 40-person sham-controlled trial found improved corneal staining after six NIR sessions, while several secondary measures were not significantly different. Results from IPL combinations are mixed and cannot isolate PBM effects.

PBM Database summary

What the records report

A 40-person sham-controlled trial found improved corneal staining after six NIR sessions, while several secondary measures were not significantly different. Results from IPL combinations are mixed and cannot isolate PBM effects.

Summary of the Evidence

The dry-eye category contains 35 publications: 26 human-tagged reports, five animal tags, one protocol, and five review-type reports. Some publications combine clinical and animal models, so these method counts overlap. Clinical designs include randomized, comparative, single-arm, retrospective, and perioperative studies. The number of distinct patient cohorts cannot be deduplicated from the source list; reports may reuse cohorts or compare one eye with the other. Park et al. 2022

Human and clinical evidence

Park et al. randomized 40 patients to near-infrared LED treatment or placebo. Six sessions over three weeks improved the primary fluorescein corneal-staining outcome at week four. Some secondary outcomes, including conjunctival staining and Schirmer testing, improved, but tear breakup time and several lid or gland measures did not differ significantly. Other reports include randomized pre- and post-cataract treatment, comparison of light therapy with intense pulsed light, and combined IPL-plus-light treatment. A 2026 randomized adjunct study found greater lipid-layer thickness with added light but no additional symptom or inflammatory benefit over IPL alone. A separate postmenopausal-women study used polychromatic Bioptron light, so it is not directly equivalent to red or near-infrared PBM.

Animal evidence

Rat, mouse, and rabbit models report changes in tear breakup time, staining, gland inflammation, or tissue markers. These models support possible mechanisms but do not establish symptomatic benefit in patients.

In-vitro and ex-vivo evidence

The source category contains no separately tagged in-vitro or ex-vivo report beyond papers that combine human and animal experiments. Cellular mechanisms are not a consistent clinical endpoint.

Treatment Parameters and Generalizability

Devices include near-infrared LEDs, red light, multiwavelength systems, polychromatic light, and combined IPL protocols. Treatment duration and frequency vary, and parameters are often incompletely reported. Because many studies bundle heat, IPL, or other treatment, effects cannot always be attributed to PBM alone.

Interpretation

Some signs and symptoms improve in small studies, but the evidence is heterogeneous and effects are not consistent across outcomes. Longer independent trials with sham controls, prespecified symptom measures, and clear device parameters are needed to establish durable benefit and a generalizable protocol.

Evidence strength in source summaryCorneal staining and tear-film signs: Limited positive signal Symptoms: Mixed Durable benefit and optimal protocol: Uncertain
Publications and records35 publications: 26 human-tagged, 5 animal tags across rat, mouse, and rabbit models, 1 study protocol, and 5 review or synthesis records.

Evidence strength rationale and next steps

The literature includes small controlled trials and many single-arm or combination-treatment reports. One sham-controlled study improved corneal staining but not several secondary measures. IPL combinations complicate attribution, outcomes and devices are heterogeneous, and long-term controlled evidence remains limited. Independent confirmation is limited.

Publication and study types

  • Tags overlap for papers combining human and animal evidence.
  • Clinical designs include randomized trials, comparisons, single-arm and retrospective studies.
  • Cohorts are not deduplicated; some paired-eye and perioperative reports may share participants.
  • One protocol has no outcome data.
